items.stem: Why classify data before writing rules about what may be entered into ChatGPT prompts?

options.text: Rules can then differ by sensitivity instead of treating all data the same
options.rationale: Correct: classification lets governance apply proportionate rules by sensitivity.

options.text: Classification makes the model answer faster
options.rationale: Classification does not affect model speed.

options.text: It removes the need for any human review
options.rationale: Classification supports, but does not replace, human review.
Classification is unrelated to context window size.

items.explanation: Correct: classification lets governance apply proportionate rules by sensitivity.

items.stem: An enterprise enables audit logging but no one examines the logs. What governance gap remains?

options.text: Logs provide no assurance unless they are reviewed and acted on
options.rationale: Correct: a control only operates if its output is reviewed; unreviewed logs give no assurance.
Logging records events; it does not by itself prevent misuse.

options.text: The gap is closed as soon as logging is on
options.rationale: Enabling logging is necessary but not sufficient without review.

options.text: Logs replace the need for access reviews
options.rationale: Logs and periodic access reviews serve different purposes.

items.explanation: Correct: a control only operates if its output is reviewed; unreviewed logs give no assurance.

items.stem: Which TWO elements belong in an access review for enterprise ChatGPT? (Select TWO)

options.text: A named owner responsible for the review
options.rationale: Correct: accountability requires a named owner.

options.text: A defined cadence, such as quarterly
options.rationale: Correct: a periodic cadence makes the review a repeatable control.
Appearance is irrelevant to access governance.

options.text: The number of emojis used in prompts

items.explanation: Correct: accountability requires a named owner.
